The weather pattern will undergo changes this week as winter finally 
begins to rear its head in the mountains over the Inland Northwest. 
A stalled out occluded front over the Cascades is already providing 
a taste with snow observed on the Stevens Pass WSDOT camera. 
Temperatures over the pass are sitting right around freezing with 
snow melting on contact with the road surface. This initial band of 
precipitation is associated with a tightly wound, vertically stacked 
are of low pressure spinning just off of the Washington coastline. 
This will be the first low pressure system that impacts the region. 
Models depict a second, nearly identical looking low pressure system 
that takes the place of this current one in the middle of the week. 
It will be an active week with the main challenge being snow levels 
and snow accumulations in the mountains.

Rest of today through Tuesday: The low pressure system will spin 
offshore over the next 12-15 hours. A potent shortwave disturbance 
rounding the low will act to back the flow pattern over the 
Northwest turning more southerly into tonight. This will have the 
effect of entraining drier air over the northern Cascades with 
precipitaiton decreasing through the morning hours on Monday before 
the low tracks east roughly along the OR/WA border. The 
shortwave round the low at this same time will supply a healthy 
dose of dynamics that will fuel frontogenesis lower in the 
atmosphere. The associated deformation band will strengthen and 
swing through from south to northeast across the area Monday 
afternoon/evening. Snow levels only drop to between 4500 to 5500
feet with this band and will bring mainly valley rain and high 
mountain snow. Best dynamics will occur across southeast WA into
the Idaho Panhandle and generally miss our highest mountain 
passes of Washington Pass in the North Cascades and Sherman 
Pass. Little impacts from precipitation is expected and will 
bring much rainfall. A modest cold pool of -23 to -25 C at 500 
mb over northeast OR into the southern ID Panhandle will 
destabilize mid levels for a 10-20% chance of thunderstorms 
primarily in the Northeast Blue Mountains to the Camas Prairie. 
Wrap around moisture that feeds into the low pushing into 
western Montana will continue to result in showers across 
extreme eastern WA and into the ID Panhandle Monday night into 
Tuesday.

Tuesday night through Thursday: This is the part of the forecast 
period when the second low pressure system will deepen along the 
west coast of WA. Reinforcing cold air dives south with the low and 
will push across the Cascades by Tuesday evening. This will cool off 
thermal profiles for snow levels to drop further down to 3,000 feet. 
A shortwave rounding at this time will ramp up precipitaiton over 
the Cascades, along with moist upslope on the western slopes that 
enhances precipitaiton over the Cascade crest. Mid levels also 
steepen quite a bit with the passage of shortwave and frontal 
band. Strong westerly flow will bring with it the potential for 
a convergence zone and the increasing instability will increase 
the risk for bursts of heavier snow into Wednesday morning. The 
Cascades mountains, and the crest in particular, will easily 
see the potential for 3 to 8 inches of snow, and near a foot of 
snow isn't of the question where the convergence zone sets up. 
The limiting factor for snow accumulation over Washington Pass 
and Stevens Pass will how quickly snow levels fall and 
temperatures cool. Road temperatures will start out warm, but 
heavier intensity snow will have a chance to overcome this. The 
NBM is showing fairly low probability of seeing 6 inches of snow
Tuesday night into Wednesday morning for these passes, but snow
covered roads and winter travel will definitely be in play and 
potential risk for travelers. Sherman Pass is also expected to 
receive snow Wednesday morning with the frontal band with around
2 to 4 inches expected.

Thursday night through Saturday: Drier air moves over the region 
Thursday night into Friday and this is expected to result in a 
decreasing trend of precipitation. The closed upper level low 
pressure system becomes cut off and remains in close proximity just 
west of the PNW. There is less confidence in the forecast details 
this far out in the period. Temperatures will be near normal and 
snow levels remaining right around 3,000 feet. There will 
continue to be a risk of disturbances rounding the low with 
precipitation at times that would bring valley rain and mountain
snow. /SVH
